script:
export const meta = {
  name: 'verify-report-claims',
  description: 'Adversarially verify every numeric/licensing/date claim the D-ANC report will cite, against primary sources',
  phases: [{ title: 'Verify', detail: '3 verifiers, ~18 claims each' }],
}

const GROUPS = {
  architectures_benchmarks: [
    'A1 DeepFilterNet2 (Schroeter et al., arXiv 2205.05474, IWAENC 2022): 2.31M params, 0.356 GMAC/s, VoiceBank+DEMAND WB-PESQ 3.08 (some sources 3.03), STOI 0.943, RTF 0.04 on i5-8250U single thread and 0.42 on Raspberry Pi 4, 2-frame look-ahead, 40 ms overall latency',
    'A2 DeepFilterNet3 (arXiv 2305.08227, Interspeech 2023 show&tell): VB+DEMAND PESQ 3.17, STOI 0.944, RTF 0.19 single-thread i5-8250U, 48 kHz',
    'A3 GTCRN (Rong et al., ICASSP 2024, github Xiaobin-Rong/gtcrn, MIT): 48.2K params, 33.0 MMAC/s, VB+DEMAND PESQ 2.87, STOI 0.940, SI-SNR 18.83 dB; HybridLoss = 30*(real+imag)+70*mag+sisnr with power-law compression 0.3',
    'A4 ULCNet (ICASSP 2024): 688K params, 0.098 GMAC/s, VB+DEMAND PESQ 2.87, RTF 0.127 on one Cortex-A53 core',
    'A5 LiSenNet (ICASSP 2025, github hyyan2k/LiSenNet): 37K params, 56 MMAC/s, VB+DEMAND PESQ 3.07',
    'A6 UL-UNAS (arXiv 2503.00340): 171K params, 35 MMAC/s, VB+DEMAND PESQ 2.96 / 3.09 with PESQ loss',
    'A7 FRCRN (ICASSP 2022): VB+DEMAND WB-PESQ 3.21, 6.9M params (16 kHz model)',
    'A8 Non-causal references on VB+DEMAND: CMGAN PESQ 3.41 (Interspeech 2022), MP-SENet 3.50 (Interspeech 2023), SEMamba 3.55 (IEEE SLT 2024)',
    'A9 BASENet (arXiv 2606.12662, June 2026, Thales): causal variant VB+DEMAND PESQ 3.44',
    'A10 DPDFNet (arXiv 2512.16420, Dec 2025, Ceva): on their multilingual low-SNR (0/5/10 dB) test set DFN3 PESQ 2.45, DPDFNet-8 PESQ 2.85, GTCRN 2.00',
    'A11 RNNoise (Valin, arXiv 1709.08243, IEEE MMSP 2018): 87,503 weights, 48 kHz, 20 ms window / 10 ms hop',
    'A12 ICASSP 2021 DNS Challenge real-time track: total algorithmic latency (frame + stride + look-ahead) <= 40 ms; per-frame processing below the stride on an Intel Core i5 quad-core 2.4 GHz',
    'A13 Tan & Wang CRN, Interspeech 2018: at -5 dB (untrained speakers, babble/cafeteria) STOI 0.7642 and PESQ 2.04 enhanced',
    'A14 Xu, Du, Huang, Dai, Lee (Interspeech 2015, arXiv 1703.07172): unseen NOISEX-92 noises (Buccaneer1, Destroyer engine, HF channel) at 5 dB enhanced STOI 0.876, PESQ 2.597; at -5 dB 0.688 / 1.887',
    'A15 Tan & Wang GCRN (IEEE/ACM TASLP 28:380-390, 2020): at 0 dB STOI 0.9012, PESQ 2.65; at -5 dB 0.8075 / 2.13',
    'A16 MetricGAN+ (Fu et al., arXiv 2104.03538, Interspeech 2021): VB+DEMAND PESQ 3.15',
    'A17 Braun & Tashev (arXiv 2009.12286, 2020): compression exponent c = 0.3 and combined compressed loss with weight 0.3 on the complex term performs best',
  ],
  edge_hybrid_standards: [
    'B1 NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin 64GB: 275 TOPS (INT8 sparse), 12-core Arm Cortex-A78AE at 2.2 GHz, 2048-core Ampere GPU with 64 Tensor Cores, 64 GB LPDDR5 at 204.8 GB/s, power 15 W - 60 W',
    'B2 Jetson Linux r36.4 developer guide nvpmodel modes for AGX Orin 64GB: MAXN (12 CPUs, 2201.6 MHz), 15W (4 CPUs, 1113.6 MHz, GPU 408 MHz), 30W (8 CPUs, 1728 MHz), 50W (12 CPUs, 1497.6 MHz)',
    'B3 TensorRT 10 docs: IRNNv2Layer removed in TensorRT 10.0; loop API supports only FP32 and FP16',
    'B4 TensorRT docs: TensorRT 10.7 was the last release supporting DLA',
    'B5 NVIDIA TensorRT-RTX docs: kernel launch takes about 5-15 microseconds of CPU/driver time per kernel',
    'B6 JetPack 7.2 (released 2026-06-02): TensorRT 10.16.2, CUDA 13.2.1, Ubuntu 24.04, adds Orin support in JetPack 7; JetPack 6.2.x: TensorRT 10.3, CUDA 12.6',
    'B7 Kealey et al. arXiv 2303.00949 (2023): Jetson Xavier NX audio I/O latency 80 ms without processing, 40 ms algorithmic',
    'B8 Widrow et al., Adaptive noise cancelling: principles and applications, Proc. IEEE 63(12):1692-1716, Dec 1975; with signal leakage into the reference the output SNR density equals the reciprocal of the reference SNR density',
    'B9 ITU-T G.114 (05/2003): below 150 ms one-way mouth-to-ear most applications are essentially transparent; 400 ms upper planning bound',
    'B10 ICASSP 2023 AEC Challenge (Cutler et al., arXiv 2309.12553): algorithmic latency + buffering latency <= 20 ms',
    'B11 Tan, Zhang, Wang, Deep learning based real-time speech enhancement for dual-microphone mobile phones, IEEE/ACM TASLP 29:1853-1863, 2021: pruned causal model 103.07K params; 2.78 ms per 20 ms frame on i7-10510U; at 0 dB diffuse babble PESQ 1.57 -> 2.74, STOI 66.48 -> 76.48 %',
    'B12 Haubner, Brendel, Kellermann, End-to-end deep learning-based adaptation control for frequency-domain adaptive system identification, ICASSP 2022, arXiv 2106.01262',
    'B13 NKF neural Kalman filter AEC (Yang et al., arXiv 2207.11388): 5.3K parameters',
    'B14 Zhang & Wang, Deep ANC, Neural Networks vol 141 pp 1-10, 2021',
    'B15 Yuan et al. arXiv 2604.05519 (Apr 2026, preprint): open-ear smart-glasses ANC median mic-to-speaker latency 113 microseconds; noise reduction 11.1 dB at 45 us vs 4.4 dB at 726 us',
    'B16 Rusci et al. arXiv 2210.07692 (2022): mixed FP16-INT8 PTQ PESQ drop 0.06; uniform 8-bit about 0.3',
    'B17 Fedorov et al. TinyLSTMs, Interspeech 2020 (arXiv 2005.11138): 0.55 dB SDR loss after pruning+quantization; 2.39 ms latency on MCU',
    'B18 ONNX Runtime quantization docs: dynamic quantization recommended for RNN/transformer models, static for CNNs',
  ],
  defence_physics_data_metrics: [
    'C1 Narain, Kant, Singh, Defence Science Journal 76(3), May 2026, pp. 408-417, DOI 10.14429/dsj.21095; abstract claims SNR gains 14-16 dB and PESQ improvements exceeding 7 %',
    'C2 Jaiswal, Yeduri, Cenkeramaddi, Int. J. Speech Technology 25(3):745-758, 2022: 8 kHz, two utterances, helicopter/airplane noise from ESC-50, PESQ 2.621 for female speaker helicopter 5 dB with implicit Wiener filter',
    'C3 Timmermann, Ernst, Sachau, Speech enhancement for helicopter headsets: simulation and implementation on an FPGA platform, POMA vol 52, 2023, DOI 10.1121/2.0001865 (metadata; PESQ 1.13 -> 2.08 if accessible)',
    'C4 MIL-STD-1474E (15 April 2015) clause 4.3: speech communication not degraded below 80 % MRT (ANSI/ASA S3.2); impulsive peak < 140 dBP at the ear',
    'C5 MIL-STD-1472H (15 Sep 2020) Table XVII: normal acceptable intelligibility 91 % MRT / AI 0.5; minimally acceptable 75 % / 0.3; clause 5.3.6.5 noise-cancelling mics >= 10 dBA improvement in very loud low-frequency noise',
    'C6 RFC 8130 (March 2017): MELPe 2400 bps uses a 22.5 ms frame of 180 samples at 8 kHz; 1200/600 bps use 3/4 frames; STANAG 4591',
    'C7 R.C. Maher, Acoustical characterization of gunshots, IEEE SAFE workshop 2007: muzzle blast typically lasts less than 3 ms',
    'C8 Meinke et al., Seminars in Hearing 2017 (PMC5634813): peak SPLs from firearms range from about 140 to 175 dB',
    'C9 US Patent 5,310,137 (Sikorsky/United Technologies): BLACK HAWK main rotor blade passing frequency approximately 17 Hz',
    'C10 Mukhutdinov, Alex, Cavallaro, Wang, IEEE Access vol 11, 2023, DOI 10.1109/ACCESS.2023.3253719: drone ego-noise at -15 dB, best model PESQ 1.0 -> 1.9, ESTOI 0.1 -> 0.4',
    'C11 Vibravox (Hauret et al., arXiv 2407.11828): at 90 dB ambient, signal-to-external-noise ratio of throat microphone 25.6 dB vs headset boom mic 0.1 dB',
    'C12 PMSQE: Martin-Donas, Gomez, Gonzalez, Peinado, IEEE Signal Processing Letters 25(11):1680-1684, 2018, DOI 10.1109/LSP.2018.2871419',
    'C13 SI-SDR: Le Roux, Wisdom, Erdogan, Hershey, SDR - half-baked or well done?, ICASSP 2019',
    'C14 STOI: Taal, Hendriks, Heusdens, Jensen, IEEE TASLP 19(7):2125-2136, 2011; ESTOI: Jensen & Taal, IEEE/ACM TASLP 24(11):2009-2022, 2016',
    'C15 ITU-T P.862 (02/2001) PESQ narrowband; ITU-T P.862.2 wideband extension (2005, revised 2007); P.862.2 output range approx 1.04 to 4.64',
    'C16 VoiceBank+DEMAND (Valentini-Botinhao et al., SSW 2016 / Interspeech 2016, Edinburgh DataShare 10283/2791): CC BY 4.0, test SNRs 17.5/12.5/7.5/2.5 dB, 824 test utterances, 2 test speakers',
    'C17 Licenses: ESC-50 CC BY-NC 3.0; LibriSpeech CC BY 4.0; UrbanSound8K CC BY-NC; github saraalemadi/DroneAudioDataset has no license file; NOISEX-92 copyright TNO 1990 distributed under NATO AC243/RSG-10',
    'C18 Nelke & Vary, Measurement, analysis and simulation of wind noise signals for mobile communication devices, IWAENC 2014',
    'C19 Friedlander waveform for blast waves p(t)=Ps(1-t/T)exp(-bt/T) (Friedlander 1946, Proc. R. Soc. A) as used for muzzle blast (e.g. Routh & Maher AES 2016)',
  ],
}

const SCHEMA = {
  type: 'object',
  properties: {
    checks: {
      type: 'array',
      items: {
        type: 'object',
        properties: {
          id: { type: 'string' },
          status: { type: 'string', enum: ['confirmed', 'corrected', 'unverifiable', 'refuted'] },
          verified_text: { type: 'string', description: 'the claim as it should be stated, with corrected numbers/dates' },
          source_url: { type: 'string' },
          source_date: { type: 'string' },
          comment: { type: 'string' },
        },
        required: ['id', 'status', 'verified_text', 'source_url', 'comment'],
      },
    },
  },
  required: ['checks'],
}

const results = await parallel(Object.entries(GROUPS).map(([g, claims]) => () =>
  agent(`You are an adversarial fact-checker for a defence speech-enhancement engineering report. Today is 2026-10-03.
Load WebSearch and WebFetch with ToolSearch (query "select:WebSearch,WebFetch"). For EACH claim below, fetch a primary source (arXiv abs/HTML page, official GitHub README/code, publisher/DOI landing page, ISCA archive, vendor docs, standards text) and check every number, date, venue and license. Status: confirmed (all details match), corrected (give the right values in verified_text), unverifiable (could not access the evidence yourself - do NOT guess), refuted. Be efficient: one or two authoritative fetches per claim. Background notes with candidate URLs exist in /Users/nsivaprasadnandyala/Desktop/DRDO_Project/docs/research/*.md (read them with the Read tool if helpful) but you must re-check against the source itself. Do not write or modify any files. Return verified_text for every claim (a precise, citable sentence including venue and date).

CLAIMS:
${claims.join('\n')}`, { label: `verify:${g}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: SCHEMA }).then(r => r ? { group: g, ...r } : null)))
return results.filter(Boolean)

checks.verified_text: DeepFilterNet2 (Schröter, Escalante-B., Rosenkranz, Maier; arXiv 2205.05474, 11 May 2022; IWAENC 2022, DOI 10.1109/IWAENC53105.2022.9914782) has 2.306M params and 0.356 GMACs, with RTF 0.04 on a notebook Core i5-8250U (average of 5 runs; the paper does not say it was single-threaded) and RTF 0.42 on a Raspberry Pi 4. On VoiceBank+DEMAND the '+Simplified DNN' configuration scores PESQ 3.08 / STOI 0.9429 (CSIG 4.30, CBAK 3.40, COVL 3.699), and the final '+Post-Filter' configuration scores PESQ 3.03 / STOI 0.941 (CSIG 3.72, CBAK 3.37, COVL 3.63). It runs at 48 kHz with 20 ms windows, 50% overlap and a 2-frame look-ahead, giving 40 ms overall algorithmic delay.
checks.comment: Params, MACs, both RTFs, look-ahead and 40 ms delay all match Table 1 and the text. Two corrections. (1) The DFN2 paper never calls its 0.04 RTF single-threaded; only RNNoise is footnoted as single-threaded. DFN3's single-threaded RTF of 0.19 on the same CPU suggests the two RTFs are not comparable. (2) 3.08 and 3.03 are two different rows: 3.08/0.9429 is without the post-filter, 3.03/0.941 is the final model with the post-filter. The DFN3 paper and the ULCNet paper both quote DFN2 as 3.08. Name the configuration whenever you quote a number. The README cites the venue as 17th IWAENC 2022, and Crossref gives the DOI above.

checks.verified_text: DeepFilterNet3 ('DeepFilterNet: Perceptually Motivated Real-Time Speech Enhancement', Schröter, Rosenkranz, Escalante-B., Maier; arXiv 2305.08227, 14 May 2023; accepted as an Interspeech 2023 show-and-tell demo) reports VoiceBank+DEMAND PESQ 3.17, CSIG 4.34, CBAK 3.61, COVL 3.77 and STOI 0.944. It has a single-threaded RTF of 0.19 on a notebook i5-8250U and runs at 48 kHz with 20 ms windows, 10 ms hop and a 2-frame look-ahead, for 40 ms overall latency.
checks.comment: Every number matches the arXiv abstract and the HTML Table 1. The paper gives no params or MACs for DFN3; the DPDFNet paper lists 2.14M / 0.35 GMACs. Code is dual MIT/Apache-2.0 per the GitHub README; check the license on the weights separately.

checks.verified_text: GTCRN (Rong, Sun, Zhang, Hu, Zhu, Lu; ICASSP 2024, pp. 971-975, DOI 10.1109/ICASSP48485.2024.10448310; MIT-licensed code at github.com/Xiaobin-Rong/gtcrn): the official README gives 48.2K params and 33.0 MMACs/s, updated from the paper's 23.7K and 39.6 MMACs/s. On VCTK-DEMAND it scores SI-SNR 18.83 dB, PESQ 2.87 and STOI 0.940. The repo's loss.py HybridLoss returns 30*(real_loss+imag_loss) + 70*mag_loss + sisnr, where the magnitude is power-law compressed with exponent 0.3 and real/imag are divided by |X|^0.7 (i.e. compressed complex with exponent 0.3).
checks.comment: README and loss.py read directly; venue, pages and DOI checked via Crossref. Minor points: the README rounds the table to 0.05M / 0.03G and states the 48.2K / 33.0 MMACs correction in text. The sisnr term in loss.py is -log10(ratio), not a 10*log10 dB value. The loss's ISTFT uses n_fft 512, hop 256 and a sqrt-Hann window.

checks.verified_text: ULCNet (Shetu, Chakrabarty, Thiergart, Mabande; arXiv 2312.08132; ICASSP 2024, pp. 466-470, DOI 10.1109/ICASSP48485.2024.10448353) has 688K params and 0.098 GMACS. The ULCNet_MS variant scores VoiceBank+DEMAND PESQ 2.87 (SI-SDR 16.89). ULCNet reaches RTF 0.127 at 16 kHz on a single core of a 1.43 GHz Cortex-A53, and RTF 0.02 on a Core i5-8250U.
checks.comment: All numbers match. Name the variant: PESQ 2.87 is ULCNet_MS, while ULCNet_Freq scores PESQ 2.54 / SI-SDR 17.20. The paper writes the Cortex-A53 result as '0.127 RTF (182MHz)'.

checks.verified_text: LiSenNet (Yan, Zhang, Fan, Zhou, Liu; arXiv 2409.13285, 20 Sep 2024; ICASSP 2025, DOI 10.1109/ICASSP49660.2025.10888272; MIT-licensed code at github.com/hyyan2k/LiSenNet) has 37k params and 56M MACs/s and scores VoiceBank+DEMAND PESQ 3.07, STOI 0.939.
checks.comment: The arXiv abstract and Table I give 37k / 56M MAC/s / PESQ 3.07 / STOI 0.939. arXiv only says 'submitted to ICASSP 2025'; Crossref confirms publication at ICASSP 2025 (pp. 1-5). The UL-UNAS paper (Table VII) marks the 3.07 result as trained with an extra PESQ loss and reports 2.95 / 0.937 without it. That annotation comes from UL-UNAS, not the LiSenNet paper.

checks.verified_text: UL-UNAS (Rong, Yang, Wang, Hu, Zhu, Chen, Lu; arXiv 2503.00340, v1 1 Mar 2025, v2 1 Feb 2026; accepted by IEEE TASLP; MIT-licensed code at github.com/Xiaobin-Rong/ul-unas) has 171k params, 35M MACs/s and 0 ms look-ahead. On VCTK-DEMAND it scores PESQ 2.96 (SI-SNR 18.25, STOI 0.941) without the PESQ loss and PESQ 3.09 (SI-SNR 18.48, STOI 0.941) with it.
checks.comment: The paper text says 'With only 35M MACS and a compact size of 171k parameters, UL-UNAS achieves a PESQ score of 3.09'. Table VII gives 2.96 (no PESQ loss) and 3.09 (with PESQ loss). Its DNS3 results are PESQ 2.30 and DNSMOS OVRL 2.71.

checks.verified_text: FRCRN (Zhao, Ma, Watcharasupat, Gan; arXiv 2206.07293; ICASSP 2022, pp. 9281-9285, DOI 10.1109/ICASSP43922.2022.9747578) scores VoiceBank+DEMAND WB-PESQ 3.21 (CSIG 4.23, CBAK 3.64, COVL 3.73). The 16 kHz wideband FRCRN has 6.9M params (Table 1, WSJ0 ablation), and the 48 kHz fullband model has 10.27M params and 12.30 GMACs/s.
checks.comment: WB-PESQ 3.21 is in Table 3 and 6.9M in Table 1 ('Objective evaluation results of various models on WSJ0 dataset', 16 kHz section). arXiv lists 'Accepted by ICASSP 2022', and Crossref gives the pages and DOI. ClearerVoice-Studio's retrained FRCRN_SE_16K lists PESQ 3.23 on VB+DEMAND; that is a different checkpoint from the paper.

checks.verified_text: Non-causal VoiceBank+DEMAND references: CMGAN (Cao, Abdulatif, Yang; arXiv 2203.15149; Interspeech 2022, pp. 936-940) PESQ 3.41. MP-SENet (Lu, Ai, Ling; arXiv 2305.13686; Interspeech 2023, pp. 3834-3838, DOI 10.21437/Interspeech.2023-1441) PESQ 3.50. SEMamba (Chao et al.; arXiv 2405.06573; IEEE SLT 2024, pp. 302-308, DOI 10.1109/SLT61566.2024.10832332) PESQ 3.55, or 3.69 with Perceptual Contrast Stretching.
checks.comment: All three values are in the arXiv abstracts: CMGAN 3.41 (journal-ref 'Proceedings of INTERSPEECH 2022, pp. 936-940'), MP-SENet 3.50 ('Accepted by Interspeech 2023'), SEMamba 3.55 ('Accepted to IEEE SLT 2024'). MP-SENet and SEMamba pages/DOIs come from Crossref. Other sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15149, https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13686.

checks.verified_text: BASENet (Martins Gomes and Capman, Thales SIX GTS, France; arXiv 2606.12662, v1 10 Jun 2026; preprint with no venue listed): the causal BASENet-3 has 0.81M params and 7.1 G MACs and scores VoiceBank+DEMAND PESQ 3.44 (CSIG 4.58, CBAK 3.85, COVL 4.04, STOI 96%). The non-causal variant (0.83M, 7.3 G MACs) scores PESQ 3.55.
checks.comment: Abstract and HTML tables match, and the HTML shows the Thales SIX GTS affiliation. The paper gives no algorithmic latency or code release. It is an unrefereed preprint; label it as such in the report.

checks.verified_text: DPDFNet (Rika, Sapir, Gus; Ceva Technologies, Israel; arXiv 2512.16420, v1 18 Dec 2025, v3 16 Jun 2026; accepted in Speech Communication, DOI 10.1016/j.specom.2026.103430): on the authors' multilingual low-SNR set (0/5/10 dB, 12 languages, 324 clips, about 13.5 h), the current accepted version (v3, Table 1) reports PESQ 2.76 for DeepFilterNet3, 3.20 for DPDFNet-8 and 2.21 for GTCRN (DeepFilterNet2 2.59). arXiv v1 had reported 2.45, 2.85 and 2.00. STOI and SI-SNR are unchanged between versions (DPDFNet-8: 93.4 / 14.47 dB).
checks.comment: The claimed values (DFN3 2.45, DPDFNet-8 2.85, GTCRN 2.00) are exactly the v1 values (18 Dec 2025, 'multilingual low-SNR test set'). The accepted v3 changes every PESQ value in that table (e.g. noisy 1.27 to 1.32, DPDFNet-8 2.85 to 3.20); v3 does not explain why. Cite v3 / the journal version, or say explicitly that you are citing v1. The ranking (DPDFNet-8 > DFN3 > GTCRN) still holds. Checked by downloading and parsing both HTML versions.

checks.verified_text: RNNoise (J.-M. Valin, 'A Hybrid DSP/Deep Learning Approach to Real-Time Full-Band Speech Enhancement'; arXiv 1709.08243; IEEE MMSP 2018, DOI 10.1109/MMSP.2018.8547084) uses 87,503 weights for 215 neural-network units, operates on 48 kHz full-band speech, and processes 20 ms Vorbis windows with 50% overlap (10 ms offset).
checks.comment: The full text says 'The size of the executable is dominated by the 87,503 weights needed to represent the 215 units' and 'The main processing loop is based on 20 ms windows with 50% overlap (10 ms offset)'. arXiv comment is 'MMSP 2018' (v3, 31 May 2018). Crossref confirms the 2018 IEEE 20th MMSP DOI.

checks.verified_text: ICASSP 2021 DNS Challenge (Reddy et al.; arXiv 2009.06122; ICASSP 2021, pp. 6623-6627, DOI 10.1109/ICASSP39728.2021.9415105), Track 1 real-time rule: total algorithmic latency (frame size T + stride Ts + any look-ahead) must be at most 40 ms, and the suppressor must process a frame in less than the stride on an Intel Core i5 quad-core at 2.4 GHz or an equivalent processor.
checks.comment: Wording matches arXiv v2 (26 Oct 2020). The paper's own examples: a 20 ms frame with 10 ms stride (30 ms) passes, while a 32 ms frame with 16 ms stride (48 ms) fails. Any 32 ms/16 ms model would therefore break this rule.

checks.verified_text: Tan & Wang, 'A Convolutional Recurrent Neural Network for Real-Time Speech Enhancement' (Interspeech 2018, pp. 3229-3233, DOI 10.21437/Interspeech.2018-1405): on untrained speakers at -5 dB, averaged over babble and cafeteria noise (WSJ0 SI-84, 16 kHz), the causal CRN scores STOI 76.42% and PESQ 2.04, up from 57.86% and 1.52 unprocessed.
checks.comment: Table 3 of the ISCA PDF: CRN at -5 dB average gives STOI 76.42 and PESQ 2.04 (babble 77.98/2.04, cafeteria 74.85/2.03). Training was about 500 h at -5 to 0 dB with 10,000 noises. The PESQ variant is not stated (ITU-T P.862 cited). The CRN has 17.58M params (Fig. 5).

checks.verified_text: Xu, Du, Huang, Dai, Lee, 'Multi-objective Learning and Mask-based Post-processing for DNN based Speech Enhancement' (Interspeech 2015, pp. 1508-1512, DOI 10.21437/Interspeech.2015-358; arXiv 1703.07172): averaged over three unseen NOISEX-92 noises (Buccaneer1, Destroyer engine, HF channel) on TIMIT at 16 kHz, the proposed MFCC+IBM+PP DNN scores PESQ 2.597 / STOI 0.876 at 5 dB and PESQ 1.887 / STOI 0.688 at -5 dB. Noisy input scores 1.793/0.772 at 5 dB and 1.235/0.541 at -5 dB.
checks.comment: Read from Table 2 of the arXiv PDF. The DNN was trained on 115 noise types, about 80 h. At -5 dB the DNN baseline scores 1.617/0.645 and LogMMSE 1.261/0.525. Interspeech venue, pages and DOI checked via Crossref.

checks.verified_text: Tan & Wang, 'Learning Complex Spectral Mapping With Gated Convolutional Recurrent Networks for Monaural Speech Enhancement' (IEEE/ACM TASLP 28:380-390, 2020; e-pub 22 Nov 2019; DOI 10.1109/TASLP.2019.2955276): on untrained speakers, averaged over babble and cafeteria noise (WSJ0 SI-84, 16 kHz), GCRN+TCS (G=2) scores STOI 90.12% / PESQ 2.65 at 0 dB and STOI 80.75% / PESQ 2.13 at -5 dB.
checks.comment: Tables II and III of the PMC author manuscript match: unprocessed is 57.84%/1.50 at -5 dB and 69.80%/1.80 at 0 dB. The text also says SNR improves by more than 12 dB at -5 dB. These are the 'GCRN + TCS' rows with group count G=2; name that configuration.

checks.verified_text: MetricGAN+ (Fu, Yu, Hsieh, Plantinga, Ravanelli, Lu, Tsao; arXiv 2104.03538; Interspeech 2021, pp. 201-205, DOI 10.21437/Interspeech.2021-599) scores VoiceBank+DEMAND PESQ 3.15, 0.3 above the original MetricGAN.
checks.comment: The abstract states PESQ 3.15 and 'Accepted by Interspeech 2021'. Crossref gives pages 201-205. The FRCRN paper's Table 3 lists the same 3.15 (CSIG 4.14, CBAK 3.16, COVL 3.64).

checks.verified_text: Braun & Tashev, 'A consolidated view of loss functions for supervised deep learning-based speech enhancement' (arXiv 2009.12286, 25 Sep 2020; published at the 44th Int. Conf. on Telecommunications and Signal Processing (TSP) 2021, pp. 72-76, DOI 10.1109/TSP52935.2021.9522648): the authors adopt the 'commonly used' compression exponent c = 0.3 rather than tuning it. Mixing compressed magnitude and compressed complex losses as (1-β)L_mag + βL_complex works best at β = 0.3, giving test PESQ 3.31 versus 3.25 for compressed magnitude only. These results come from a 2.8M-param GRU model on reverberant CHiME-2 WSJ-20k.
checks.comment: β = 0.3 on the complex term is confirmed (Sec. 5.2, Fig. 3, Table 2). Correction: c = 0.3 was not shown to be optimal. Sec. 3.4 only calls it 'a commonly used compression exponent'; no sweep over c was run, so do not say c = 0.3 'performs best'. Also, β was chosen by grid search on validation PESQ using a reverberant dataset, and compressed fully-complex loss alone (β = 1) degrades badly (PESQ 2.88). Crossref gives the TSP 2021 venue.

checks.verified_text: Per NVIDIA's Jetson Orin product page (accessed 2026-10-03), the Jetson AGX Orin 64GB module delivers 275 TOPS (listed as '275 SPARSE INT8 TOPS' in the page's compute comparison), with a 2048-core NVIDIA Ampere GPU with 64 Tensor Cores (1.3 GHz max), a 12-core Arm Cortex-A78AE v8.2 64-bit CPU (2.2 GHz max), 64 GB 256-bit LPDDR5 at 204.8 GB/s, and a 15 W - 60 W power range.
checks.comment: All values match the official spec table. The page lists the 275 TOPS figure as sparse INT8 in its compute comparison section. Extra detail: GPU max clock 1.3 GHz; the DLA row shows 105 sparse / 52.5 dense INT8 TOPS.

checks.verified_text: NVIDIA Jetson Linux Developer Guide r36.4 ('Platform Power and Performance') lists these nvpmodel modes for Jetson AGX Orin 64GB: MAXN (ID 0) has 12 CPUs online at 2201.6 MHz max, 8 GPU TPCs at 1301 MHz and DLA at 1600 MHz; 15W (ID 1) has 4 CPUs at 1113.6 MHz, 3 TPCs at 408 MHz and DLA at 614.4 MHz; 30W (ID 2, the default) has 8 CPUs at 1728 MHz, 4 TPCs at 612 MHz and DLA at 1369.6 MHz; 50W (ID 3) has 12 CPUs at 1497.6 MHz, 8 TPCs at 816 MHz and DLA at 1369.6 MHz.
checks.comment: All the stated CPU counts and clocks match, as does the 15W GPU clock of 408 MHz. The guide states that 30W (mode ID 2) is the default mode.

checks.verified_text: The NVIDIA TensorRT 10.x documentation ('Working with Loops', latest 10.16.1) says 'IRNNv2Layer was deprecated in TensorRT 7.2.1 and was removed in TensorRT 10.0' and 'The loop API supports only FP32 and FP16 precision.'
checks.comment: Both statements appear word for word in the 10.x docs. Caveat: the current TensorRT 11.3 version of this page drops both. It no longer mentions IRNNv2Layer and now says loop precisions 'are determined by the precisions supported by its constituent body layers, not by the loop API itself.' Cite the 10.x page specifically.

checks.verified_text: NVIDIA TensorRT 11.3.0 documentation ('Working with DLA' and the 'Migrating TensorRT from 10.x to 11.x on Jetson/JetPack' guide) states 'TensorRT 10.7 was the last release that supported DLA', that DLA is not supported in TensorRT 11.0-11.3, and advises 'Use TensorRT 10.7 if DLA is required on Jetson.'
checks.comment: Confirmed in the TensorRT 11.3.0 docs and the Jetson migration guide (https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/tensorrt/11.3.0/api/migration/tensorrt-10x-to-11x-jetson.html). The 10.x (10.16.1) DLA page does not carry this statement. Implication: JetPack 7.2 ships TensorRT 10.16.2, which is after 10.7, so DLA offload through TensorRT should not be assumed on JetPack 7.2. JetPack 6.2.x ships TensorRT 10.3 (DLA 3.14).

checks.verified_text: NVIDIA TensorRT-RTX documentation ('Optimizing TensorRT-RTX Performance') states that for enqueue-bound workloads 'most CUDA kernels take the CPU and the driver around 5-15 microseconds to launch per kernel', and recommends CUDA Graphs to reduce this overhead.
checks.comment: The quote matches. Caveat: this is TensorRT-RTX documentation for desktop RTX GPUs, not Jetson. Launch overhead on an Orin Arm CPU may differ and should be measured on the board.

checks.verified_text: NVIDIA's JetPack 7.2 archive page gives a release date of 2 June 2026 and lists Jetson Linux 39.2, kernel 6.8, Ubuntu 24.04, CUDA 13.2.1, cuDNN 9.20.0 and TensorRT 10.16.2. It states that the release 'Adds support for the Jetson Orin product family within JetPack 7 releases.' JetPack 6.2.x (for example 6.2.3: Jetson Linux 36.5.2, Ubuntu 22.04) ships CUDA 12.6 (12.6.10) and TensorRT 10.3 (10.3.0).
checks.comment: JetPack 7.2 values are confirmed from the archive page. JetPack 6.2.x values are confirmed from https://developer.nvidia.com/embedded/jetpack-sdk-623 (no release date shown there). Exact JetPack 6.2.3 versions are CUDA 12.6.10, cuDNN 9.3.0 and TensorRT 10.3.0.

checks.verified_text: Kealey et al., 'Real-time Audio Video Enhancement with a Microphone Array and Headphones', arXiv:2303.00949 (2 Mar 2023; submitted to IROS 2023), run processing on a Jetson Xavier NX. They report microphone-to-playback latency 'without processing' of 80 ms, algorithmic latency of 40 ms, and 120 ms in total.
checks.comment: The 80 ms I/O latency, 40 ms algorithmic latency and Jetson Xavier NX are all stated in the full text. The authors blame the 80 ms on the USB audio path, which GPIO/I2S audio could reduce. This is a preprint 'submitted to IROS 2023', not a confirmed IROS publication.

checks.verified_text: Widrow et al., 'Adaptive noise cancelling: Principles and applications', Proc. IEEE, vol. 63, no. 12, pp. 1692-1716, Dec. 1975 (DOI 10.1109/PROC.1975.10036). They show that with an unconstrained adaptive solution and mutually correlated primary and reference noises, signal leakage into the reference makes the output signal-to-noise density ratio 'simply the reciprocal at all frequencies' of the reference-input signal-to-noise density ratio.
checks.comment: Checked against the OCR text of the author-hosted scan. The running header reads 'PROCEEDINGS OF THE IEEE, VOL. 63, NO. 12, DECEMBER 1975' and the pages run 1692-1716. The reciprocal result is in the leakage analysis (Eq. 37) and holds only under the unconstrained-Wiener and correlated-noise assumptions; include them when citing. The paper's array example reports -20 dB SNR at the reference element and +20 dB at the output. The IEEE Xplore landing page (doc 1451965) could not be rendered.

checks.verified_text: ITU-T Recommendation G.114 (05/2003), 'One-way transmission time' (approved 6 May 2003, in force), says that if end-to-end ('mouth-to-ear') delays are kept below 150 ms, 'most applications, both speech and non-speech, will experience essentially transparent interactivity'. It also recommends not exceeding a one-way delay of 400 ms for general network planning.
checks.comment: The ITU page confirms the title and 'in force' status. Text was checked against a full copy of the recommendation (cs.columbia.edu mirror of T-REC-G.114-200305). Nuance: the 400 ms figure is a network-planning (UNI-to-UNI) bound. The recommendation also notes that highly interactive tasks can be affected below 100 ms.

checks.verified_text: Cutler et al., 'ICASSP 2023 Acoustic Echo Cancellation Challenge', arXiv:2309.12553 (22 Sep 2023), require 'Algorithmic latency + buffering latency <= 20ms', reduced from 40 ms in the ICASSP 2022 challenge.
checks.comment: Authors: Cutler, Saabas, Parnamaa, Purin, Indenbom, Ristea, Guzvin, Gamper, Braun, Aichner. The 20 ms limit and the reduction from 40 ms are both stated.

checks.verified_text: Tan, Zhang and Wang, 'Deep Learning Based Real-time Speech Enhancement for Dual-microphone Mobile Phones', IEEE/ACM TASLP, vol. 29, pp. 1853-1863, 2021 (DOI 10.1109/TASLP.2021.3082318). Their pruned causal model C-DC-CRN-RI-P6 has 103.07 K parameters and processes a 20 ms frame in 2.78 ms on average on an Intel Core i7-10510U @ 1.80 GHz. In Table I (simulated reverberant diffuse babble), at 0 dB SNR it raises PESQ from 1.73 to 2.94 and STOI from 72.08% to 92.64%. In Table II (real-recorded signals), at 0 dB it raises PESQ from 1.91 to 2.76 and STOI from 78.96% to 92.99%.
checks.comment: Venue, volume, pages, the 103.07 K parameters (down from 290.44 K) and 2.78 ms per 20 ms frame on the i7-10510U all match. The claimed PESQ 1.57 -> 2.74 and STOI 66.48 -> 76.48% are wrong: neither value pair appears anywhere in the article. I parsed every table in the PMC full text (author manuscript). Correct 0 dB values are given above. Other Table I SNRs for P6: -5 dB PESQ 1.49->2.51, STOI 58.71->86.45%; 5 dB 2.04->3.27, STOI 83.53->95.88%; 10 dB 2.38->3.51, STOI 91.41->97.47%.

checks.verified_text: Haubner, Brendel and Kellermann, 'End-To-End Deep Learning-Based Adaptation Control for Frequency-Domain Adaptive System Identification', accepted for IEEE ICASSP 2022 (Singapore), arXiv:2106.01262 (v1 2 Jun 2021, v3 4 Mar 2022).
checks.comment: The title, authors and ICASSP 2022 venue match the arXiv comments field. arXiv lists no journal-ref.

checks.verified_text: Yang, Jiang, Wu, Fang and Cao, 'Low-Complexity Acoustic Echo Cancellation with Neural Kalman Filtering', arXiv:2207.11388 (v1 23 Jul 2022, v2 30 Oct 2022; accepted at ICASSP 2023 per the authors' GitHub README), report an NKF model size of 'merely 5.3 K' with a real-time factor of 0.09.
checks.comment: The 5.3 K model size and RTF 0.09 come from the abstract. The abstract does not say which hardware the RTF was measured on. The README (https://github.com/fjiang9/NKF-AEC) says 'Accepted by ICASSP 2023' and expects 16 kHz audio; the fetched README showed no license.

checks.verified_text: Zhang and Wang, 'Deep ANC: A deep learning approach to active noise control', Neural Networks, vol. 141, pp. 1-10, 2021 (DOI 10.1016/j.neunet.2021.03.037; PMID 33839375; PMC8328877).
checks.comment: The title, authors (Hao Zhang, DeLiang Wang), journal, volume, pages and year all match the PMC record.

checks.verified_text: Yuan et al., 'Active noise cancellation on open-ear smart glasses', arXiv:2604.05519 (v1 7 Apr 2026, v2 10 Sep 2026; preprint, not peer reviewed), report a median microphone-to-speaker latency of 113 us with 45 us of fixed computation. Noise reduction degrades from 11.1 dB at 45 us to 4.4 dB at 726 us.
checks.comment: All three numbers appear word for word in v1 and in the revised v2 (https://arxiv.org/html/2604.05519v2). The abstract gives mean noise reduction of 9.6 dB without calibration and 11.2 dB with brief user calibration. Authors: Kuang Yuan, Freddy Yifei Liu, Tong Xiao, Yiwen Song, Chengyi Shen, Saksham Bhutani, Justin Chan, Swarun Kumar.

checks.verified_text: Rusci, Fariselli, Croome, Paci and Flamand, 'Accelerating RNN-based Speech Enhancement on a Multi-Core MCU with Mixed FP16-INT8 Post-Training Quantization', ITEM Workshop 2022 at ECML-PKDD 2022, arXiv:2210.07692 (14 Oct 2022). They report that uniform 8-bit quantization 'degrades the PESQ score by 0.3 on average' while their mixed FP16-INT8 PTQ degrades it by 'only 0.06'.
checks.comment: Matches the abstract. The degradation is relative to FP16 baselines for LSTM/GRU models of up to 1.24 M parameters, trained on the Valentini dataset, on a 1+8-core RISC-V MCU.

checks.verified_text: Fedorov et al., 'TinyLSTMs: Efficient Neural Speech Enhancement for Hearing Aids', Interspeech 2020, pp. 4054-4058 (DOI 10.21437/Interspeech.2020-1864; arXiv:2005.11138, 20 May 2020), report 0.55 dB SDR loss for their pruned INT8 model (BSS SDR 12.77 -> 12.22 dB, with 11.9x smaller size and 2.9x fewer operations). The 2.39 ms computational latency belongs to a different model, the pruned skip-RNN INT8 variant. That figure is an average on an STM32F746VE (216 MHz Arm Cortex-M7), excludes STFT/Mel cost, and comes with BSS SDR of 12.07 dB, a 0.70 dB loss.
checks.comment: Both numbers appear in the abstract, but Table 2 shows they come from different models. The 0.55 dB loss is 'Pruned (INT8) 2' (latency 4.26 ms). The 2.39 ms (marked as an average due to skip-RNN stochasticity) is 'Pruned Skip RNN (INT8)', which loses 0.70 dB SDR. Do not present 0.55 dB and 2.39 ms as one operating point.

checks.verified_text: The ONNX Runtime quantization documentation states: 'In general, it is recommended to use dynamic quantization for RNNs and transformer-based models, and static quantization for CNN models.'
checks.comment: The quote matches the current ONNX Runtime docs.

checks.verified_text: Narain V., Kant R., Singh B.P., "Artificial Intelligence Driven Advances in Noise Cancellation: A Comprehensive Review on Overcoming Noise Hazards in Military Operations", Defence Science Journal 76(3), May 2026, pp. 408-417, DOI 10.14429/dsj.21095 (received 23 May 2025, revised 30 Oct 2025, accepted 20 Apr 2026, online 29 Apr 2026). The abstract of this review says that recent CRN- and GAN-based noise suppression models have shown SNR gains of up to 14-16 dB and PESQ improvements exceeding 7 %.
checks.comment: I checked the landing page and the PDF first-page header, which reads "Defence Science Journal, Vol. 76, No. 3, May 2026, pp. 408-417". This is a survey paper, so the 14-16 dB and >7 % figures summarise other people's work rather than new results. The abstract says 'up to 14 dB - 16 dB'. Affiliations: Thapar Institute and DRDO-DEAL Dehradun.

checks.verified_text: Jaiswal R.K., Yeduri S.R., Cenkeramaddi L.R., "Single-channel speech enhancement using implicit Wiener filter for high-quality speech communication", Int. J. Speech Technology 25(3):745-758, Sept 2022 (online 1 Aug 2022), DOI 10.1007/s10772-022-09987-4, CC BY 4.0. The test set is two narrowband 8 kHz utterances (one male, one female, average about 3 s). Helicopter and airplane noise came from Piczak's ESC dataset (ESC-50), added at 0, 2.5 and 5 dB SNR. For the female speaker with helicopter noise at 5 dB, the implicit Wiener filter scored PESQ 2.621, against 1.955 for spectral subtraction (Table 9).
checks.comment: I read the full PDF text and Table 9, and checked metadata on Crossref. The paper names the source as the 'environmental sound classification (ESC) dataset (Piczak, 2015)'. The airplane class exists only in ESC-50, not ESC-10. The paper does not tabulate unprocessed (noisy) PESQ, so the comparison is only IWF vs spectral subtraction. With n=2 utterances the statistics are weak. The male helicopter 5 dB case is IWF 2.338.

checks.verified_text: Timmermann J., Ernst F., Sachau D., "Speech enhancement for helicopter headsets: Simulation and implementation on an FPGA platform", Proceedings of Meetings on Acoustics vol. 52, art. 055004 (2023; DOI registered 10 Apr 2024), 185th Meeting of the Acoustical Society of America, Sydney, Dec 2023, DOI 10.1121/2.0001865. Method: dual-microphone, dual-stage spectral subtraction plus Wiener filter, tested on in-flight helicopter cabin recordings and validated on an FPGA. The reported PESQ 1.13 -> 2.08 comes only from the secondary DSJ review (Narain et al. 2026, Table 1); I could not check it against the POMA paper itself.
checks.comment: I confirmed the metadata through Crossref: title, authors, POMA vol 52, page/article 055004, 185th ASA Sydney. The AIP/Scitation full text and the openHSU record both returned HTTP 403, so the PESQ 1.13 -> 2.08 was NOT verified at the primary source. I did find it in the DSJ review PDF (Table 1 and text). Cite it as 'as reported by Narain et al. (2026)'.

checks.verified_text: MIL-STD-1474E (15 April 2015, superseding MIL-STD-1474D of 12 Feb 1997), clause 4.3: sound pressure levels at listener positions shall not degrade speech communication below 80 percent correct (adjusted for guessing) on the Modified Rhyme Test per ANSI/ASA S3.2. Clause 4.3.1 adds that predicted intelligibility for the worst nominal case shall be at least equivalent to 85 % MRT. The 140 dBP impulsive-noise limit is in clause 4.2.1, not 4.3: steady-state levels < 85 dBA and peak impulsive levels < 140 dBP at the ear, protected or unprotected, at all personnel locations during normal operations.
checks.comment: I read the full PDF text (Distribution A). The numbers are correct, but the claim puts the 140 dBP limit under clause 4.3; it belongs to clause 4.2.1 (Noise hazard). The 80 % MRT figure is 'adjusted for guessing' (MRT % = 2.4 x correct - 20). Table I maps 80 % MRT to AI 0.35, STI 0.36, SII 0.42.

checks.verified_text: MIL-STD-1472H (15 September 2020), Table XVII 'Intelligibility criteria for voice communication systems': exceptionally high intelligibility 97 % MRT / AI 0.7; normal acceptable 91 % / 0.5; minimally acceptable for mechanized-equipment users 80 % / 0.4; minimally acceptable 75 % / 0.3. Clause 5.3.6.5 (very loud low-frequency noise, 100 dBA overall) requires noise-cancelling microphones (5.3.6.5.1). Clause 5.3.6.5.2 requires them to improve the peak-speech to RMS-noise ratio by at least 10 dBA over non-noise-cancelling microphones of equivalent transmission characteristics.
checks.comment: I read the full PDF text. All values match. The precise sub-clause for the >= 10 dBA requirement is 5.3.6.5.2, and it applies at 100 dBA overall. Clause 5.3.11.2 says Table XVII criteria shall be used. Clause 5.3.6.4 also requires a 300 Hz high-pass filter in predominantly low-frequency noise, which may be relevant to the design.

checks.verified_text: RFC 8130 (Demjanenko & Satterlee, VOCAL Technologies, Standards Track, March 2017), 'RTP Payload Format for the MELPe Codec': MELPe (STANAG 4591) supports 2400, 1200 and 600 bps. The 2400 bps vocoder uses a 22.5 ms frame of 180 samples at 8000 Hz, 16-bit. The 1200 and 600 bps vocoders use three and four 22.5 ms frames respectively (67.5 ms and 90 ms).
checks.comment: I read the RFC text directly, and every detail matches.

checks.verified_text: R.C. Maher, "Acoustical Characterization of Gunshots", Proc. IEEE Workshop on Signal Processing Applications for Public Security and Forensics (SAFE 2007), Washington DC, 11-13 April 2007, pp. 109-113, DOI 10.1109/IEEECONF12259.2007.4218954. The paper states that the muzzle blast typically lasts for less than 3 milliseconds.
checks.comment: I read the author's PDF, and the sentence is in Section I. IEEE Xplore paginates the paper as 1-5, while the printed proceedings use 109-113.

checks.verified_text: Meinke D.K., Finan D.S., Flamme G.A., Murphy W.J., Stewart M., Lankford J.E., Tasko S., "Prevention of Noise-Induced Hearing Loss from Recreational Firearms", Seminars in Hearing 38(4):267-281, Nov 2017 (online 10 Oct 2017), DOI 10.1055/s-0037-1606323, PMC5634813. It states that peak SPLs from firearms range from about 140 to 175 dB, with most common firearms between 150 and 165 dB peak.
checks.comment: I checked the PMC full text and Crossref metadata, and both match.

checks.verified_text: US Patent 5,310,137, "Helicopter active noise control system" (Yoerkie Jr., Welsh, Sheehy; assignee United Technologies Corp., parent of Sikorsky; filed 16 Apr 1992, granted 10 May 1994). It states that the four-bladed BLACK HAWK main rotor has a blade passing frequency of approximately 17 Hz, and the S-76 approximately 19 Hz.
checks.comment: I checked Google Patents and the quoted sentence matches. The current assignee is listed as RTX Corp.

checks.verified_text: Mukhutdinov D., Alex A., Cavallaro A., Wang L., "Deep Learning Models for Single-Channel Speech Enhancement on Drones", IEEE Access vol. 11, pp. 22993-23007, 2023, DOI 10.1109/ACCESS.2023.3253719 (CC BY 4.0). The paper evaluates twelve DNNs at input SNRs from -30 to 0 dB. The best model, a time-frequency complex-domain UNet, improves ESTOI from 0.1 to 0.4, PESQ from 1.0 to 1.9 and SI-SDR from -15 to 3.7 dB at -15 dB input SNR.
checks.comment: I checked the abstract via DOAJ and the metadata (pages, license) via Crossref. All numbers match.

checks.verified_text: Hauret J. et al., "Vibravox: A Dataset of French Speech Captured with Body-conduction Audio Sensors", arXiv:2407.11828 (v1 16 Jul 2024; v4 27 Mar 2025; CC BY 4.0). Table II gives signal-to-external-noise ratios at 90 dB ambient noise: 25.6 dB for the throat microphone (iXradio XVTM822D-D35 laryngophone) and 0.1 dB for the headset boom microphone (Shure WH20XLR cardioid). The authors note these are lower bounds because of the Lombard effect.
checks.comment: I checked the v4 HTML and found Table II and the methodology text. The ratio is derived as signal-to-self-noise minus external-noise-to-self-noise, not measured directly. The arXiv page lists no journal venue. Other sensors: in-ear 4.0/3.9 dB, forehead accelerometer -3.5 dB, temple pickup 8.9 dB. The headset mic still gave the best phonemizer results in noise.

checks.verified_text: Martin-Donas J.M., Gomez A.M., Gonzalez J.A., Peinado A.M., "A Deep Learning Loss Function Based on the Perceptual Evaluation of the Speech Quality" (PMSQE), IEEE Signal Processing Letters 25(11):1680-1684, Nov 2018, DOI 10.1109/LSP.2018.2871419.
checks.comment: Crossref metadata matches every detail.

checks.verified_text: Le Roux J., Wisdom S., Erdogan H., Hershey J.R., "SDR - Half-baked or Well Done?", Proc. IEEE ICASSP 2019 (Brighton, UK, May 2019), pp. 626-630, DOI 10.1109/ICASSP.2019.8683855; preprint arXiv:1811.02508.
checks.comment: Crossref confirms the ICASSP 2019 venue, the authors and pp. 626-630.

checks.verified_text: STOI: Taal C.H., Hendriks R.C., Heusdens R., Jensen J., "An Algorithm for Intelligibility Prediction of Time-Frequency Weighted Noisy Speech", IEEE Trans. Audio, Speech, Lang. Process. 19(7):2125-2136, Sept 2011, DOI 10.1109/TASL.2011.2114881. ESTOI: Jensen J., Taal C.H., "An Algorithm for Predicting the Intelligibility of Speech Masked by Modulated Noise Maskers", IEEE/ACM TASLP 24(11):2009-2022, Nov 2016, DOI 10.1109/TASLP.2016.2585878.
checks.comment: I checked both papers on Crossref (ESTOI at https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1109/TASLP.2016.2585878). All volumes, issues and pages match.

checks.verified_text: ITU-T P.862 (02/2001) defines PESQ for narrowband telephone networks and codecs. ITU-T P.862.2 is its wideband (50-7000 Hz) extension, first approved 11/2005 and revised 13 Nov 2007 (Corrigendum 1, 10/2017). P.862.2 maps raw PESQ scores (-0.5 to 4.5) to MOS-LQO with y = 0.999 + 4.0/(1 + exp(-1.3669x + 3.8224)), which gives an output range of about 1.04 to 4.64. ITU-T has marked P.862, P.862.1, P.862.2 and P.862.3 as out of date, deleted on 5 January 2024, and refers users to P.863 (POLQA).
checks.comment: I checked the ITU P.862 and P.862.2 pages and the P.862.2 (11/2007) PDF, section 6.2, eq. 6-1. The 1.04-4.64 range is not printed in the standard; I computed it from eq. 6-1 at the raw-score limits (1.043 and 4.644). Important: the whole P.862 family is now withdrawn, so the report should say so. PESQ-WB tops out at about 4.64 and narrowband raw P.862 at 4.5.

checks.verified_text: Valentini-Botinhao C. (creator), 'Noisy speech database for training speech enhancement algorithms and TTS models' (VoiceBank+DEMAND), University of Edinburgh DataShare, hdl 10283/2791, DOI 10.7488/ds/2117, available 21 Aug 2017, licensed CC BY 4.0, 48 kHz. Companion papers: Valentini-Botinhao et al., Interspeech 2016 (28-speaker set) and SSW 2016 (56-speaker set). The test set uses two speakers from England (one male, one female), five DEMAND noises, and SNRs of 17.5, 12.5, 7.5 and 2.5 dB (20 conditions). It contains 824 test files, a count stated by Pascual et al. (SEGAN, Interspeech 2017).
checks.comment: I checked dc.rights on the DataShare REST API, which reads 'Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International Public License'. I checked the test-set SNRs and speakers in the SSW 2016 paper (ISCA archive PDF, Section 3). The 824 count does not appear in the dataset papers; I verified it in SEGAN (arXiv:1703.09452, Section 5.1). The SSW paper links the superseded version DOI 10.7488/ds/1356 (hdl 10283/1942).

checks.verified_text: ESC-50 (Piczak 2015) is released under Creative Commons Attribution Non-Commercial (CC BY-NC 3.0), with its ESC-10 subset under CC BY. LibriSpeech (OpenSLR SLR12) is CC BY 4.0. UrbanSound8K (Salamon, Jacoby, Bello 2014) is released for non-commercial research under CC BY-NC; its Zenodo record 1203745 lists CC BY-NC 4.0. The GitHub repo saraalemadi/DroneAudioDataset has no LICENSE file (GitHub API license: null), and its 'Unknown' class reuses ESC-50 clips plus Speech Commands white noise. NOISEX-92 recordings are 'copyright TNO, Soesterberg, Feb. 1990', distributed as NOISE-ROM-0 under NATO AC243/(Panel 3)/RSG-10 and ESPRIT project 2589-SAM.
checks.comment: Sources: ESC-50 README License section; openslr.org/12; Zenodo API record 1203745 plus J. Salamon's 23 Oct 2014 auditory.org posting ('Creative Commons Attribution Noncommercial License'); GitHub API for DroneAudioDataset (repo holds only README and two data folders, no license); SPIB/NOISEX page mirrored at spib.linse.ufsc.br/noise.html. The UrbanSound8K version is inconsistent: Zenodo says 4.0, while the README is reported to say 3.0 (I did not check the README myself). ESC-50 and UrbanSound8K are non-commercial only, and DroneAudioDataset inherits ESC-50's NC terms, which matters for a defence deployment.

checks.verified_text: Nelke C.M., Vary P., "Measurement, analysis and simulation of wind noise signals for mobile communication devices", Proc. 14th International Workshop on Acoustic Signal Enhancement (IWAENC 2014), Juan-les-Pins, France, 8-11 Sept 2014, pp. 327-331, DOI 10.1109/IWAENC.2014.6954312.
checks.comment: Crossref confirms the authors, title and venue. The background notes give 'Sophia Antipolis, pp. 328-332', but Crossref/IEEE give Juan-les-Pins and pp. 327-331, so the report should use the Crossref values.

checks.verified_text: The muzzle-blast impulse can be modelled with the (modified) Friedlander waveform p(t) = Ps(1 - t/T+)exp(-b t/T+) for t >= 0, where T+ is the positive-phase duration and b the decay coefficient. Secondary sources conventionally trace this waveform to F.G. Friedlander, "The diffraction of sound pulses I. Diffraction by a semi-infinite plane", Proc. R. Soc. Lond. A 186(1006):322-344, 24 Sept 1946, DOI 10.1098/rspa.1946.0046; the commonly cited original form has b = 1, and the decay coefficient b belongs to the later 'modified' form. Routh & Maher (AES 141st Convention, Los Angeles, 29 Sep-2 Oct 2016) describe the muzzle blast qualitatively as a Friedlander wave (over-pressure then under-pressure, total duration T = a + b + c), following Hamernik & Hsueh (JASA 90(1):189-196, 1991). They do not give the equation.
checks.comment: I read the Routh & Maher PDF; it uses the Friedlander concept for muzzle-blast duration but contains no equation. I verified the Friedlander 1946 citation on Crossref, but the Royal Society full text returned 403, so I could not confirm the exact formula in the 1946 paper. The equation with an explicit b should be cited as the modified Friedlander equation, and the citation should not suggest Routh & Maher use that formula.

summary: Adversarially verify every numeric/licensing/date claim the D-ANC report will cite, against primary sources

workflowProgress.promptPreview:
